content:
- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates downside risk; add buffer for sharp drops or adjust downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and overshoots; cap forecast peak and introduce early mean-reversion decay.
- In high-sentiment, high-price environments (e.g., 2023 Q1), model often fails to account for mean reversion; apply downward drag to forecast tail (last 5–7 days).
- If sentiment is flat (0.00) or neutral, model tends to drift toward historical mean; use recent volatility-adjusted moving average to anchor forecast.
- Model underestimates true volatility in low-sentiment periods; increase forecast variance or add stochastic noise if sentiment is stable but price diverges.
- When true outcome shows strong downward trend after a peak, model often fails to recognize it; apply exponential decay to forecast slope post-peak.
- In multi-day event windows (e.g., policy changes, ETS auctions), model often ignores sentiment shift; align forecast with sentiment pivot point, not just historical mean.
